peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Dear editor,
We are grateful for the opportunity to submit a revised version of our manuscript,
“Time-resolved multiomics profiling reveals the role of chromatin O-GlcNAc
modification in shaping the senescence-associated transcriptional program”
(NCOMMS-25-41520). We thank you, the three reviewers, and the co-reviewer for the
thoughtful and constructive comments that substantially improved our study.
In this revision, we performed extensive new experiments, added missing controls,
clarified methods and analyses in depth, corrected textual inaccuracies, improved figure
quality, and strengthened statistics across datasets. We believe the revised manuscript
addresses all major and minor concerns and now presents a much stronger and more
reproducible body of work. Below, we summarize the main changes and how they
address the reviewers’ points. A point-by-point response is included in the Response to
Reviewers.
Summary of Substantive Revisions
 Enhanced senescence validation across experiments
 Increased biological replicates and strengthened statistics
 Added missing controls and clarified fractionation
 Clarified computational pipelines and interpretations
 Molecular dynamics simulations — robustness and clarity
 Corrected novelty statements and improved MS evidence
 In vivo tumor studies — quantification and interpretation
 Textual and figure quality improvements
We sincerely thank you and the reviewers for the constructive guidance. We hope
that the breadth of new data, strengthened controls, methodological clarity, and rigorous
statistics now meet Nature Communications’ standards. We would be grateful for
further consideration of our revised manuscript.
Sincerely,
Yubo Liu, PhD
on behalf of all authors
Response to Reviewers
Reviewer 1#
1. In several parts of the manuscript where senescence has been assessed (eg Fig 1a,
d, Fig 7a, Fig 8e and Extended Data Fig 1) this has been done only via SA-β-Gal staining
alone, which however, in light of recent advancements in the field, is no longer
sufficient to conclusively demonstrate senescence, as it is frequently accompanied by
false positives-negatives. The authors should instead follow the revised recommended
guidelines for senescence detection (Gorgoulis et al., 2019; Ogrodnik et al., 2024).
According to the guidelines, initial screening for senescence using SA-β-Gal and/or
lipofuscin staining is expected, followed by verification of senescence via absence of
key proliferation markers, preferably MKI67, and the expression (p16INK4A,
p21WAF1/Cip1) or loss (LMNB1) of hallmark senescence markers, as also published
by Kohli et al., 2021.
Reply：
We appreciate the reviewer’s focus on whether the senescence markers employed
are sufficient to substantiate the occurrence of cellular senescence. As correctly noted,
molecular hallmarks of senescence have been refined in recent years. We have carefully
considered the reviewer’s suggestions, consulted the cited literature, and incorporated
the recommended markers to strengthen our evidence.
a) We originally used SA-β-Gal staining as an initial screening assay for senescence.
b) In the revised manuscript, we have added MKI67 as a proliferation marker in Fig.
1f, Fig. 1g, Extended Data Fig. 1c, Extended Data Fig. 1h, Extended Data Fig. 2c,
Fig. 7d. As shown, MKI67 is absent in senescent cells.
c) We had previously examined changes in p16INK4A, p21WAF1/Cip1, and p53 during the
senescence process. In the revision, we now include these markers systematically
across all senescence experiments (Fig. 1f, Fig. 1g, Extended Data Fig. 1c,
Extended Data Fig. 1h, Fig. 7d, Fig. 8e).
d) We additionally incorporated LMNB1, a recognized hallmark of senescence.
Consistent with established literature, LMNB1 expression is reduced during the
senescence progression observed in our models (Fig. 1f, Fig. 1g, Extended Data
Fig. 1c, Extended Data Fig. 1h, Extended Data Fig. 2c, Fig. 7d). In Fig. 8e, because
the mouse model involved co-injecting A549 cancer cells together with OIS
LU‑RAS cells expressing JUN and GATAD2A variants, the immunoblotting of
tumor samples reflects a mixture of A549 and LU‑RAS cells. Consequently, SASP
factors secreted by the OIS cells enhanced the proliferation of A549 cells (which
constitute the majority of the tumor mass), resulting in higher MKI67 and LMNB1
expression in the A549+LU‑RAS/Vehicle and A549+LU‑RAS/KD‑WT groups
compared to A549 and A549+LU‑RAS/KD‑AA groups.
e) Furthermore, we assessed cell-cycle alterations associated with senescence by flow
cytometry (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Fig. 1g, Extended Data Fig. 2a, Fig. 7b), and
we evaluated proliferative capacity using CCK-8 assays (Extended Data Fig. 1b,
Extended Data Fig. 1e, Extended Data Fig. 2d, Extended Data Fig. 20c) and EdU
incorporation (Fig. 1e, Extended Data Fig. 1d, Extended Data Fig. 1i, Extended
Data Fig. 2b, Extended Data Fig. 20d).
Collectively, these results provide convergent and robust evidence that the
senescent phenotypes observed in our study are genuine. Importantly, modulation of
cellular O-GlcNAcylation—particularly on the key regulators JUN and GATAD2A—
exerts a measurable impact on senescence phenotypes.
2. A very serious concern that pertains to most of the displayed results in the manuscript
is the lack of robust statistical validation, as most of the shown experiments are
representative of “at least two” or just two biological replicates. This implies that the
presented results may be largely inconclusive. The authors should increase the number
of biological replicates (and this should be reflected in their statistical analyses which
should be displayed for all major observations).
Reply：
We thank the reviewer for highlighting the number of biological replicates and the
statistical robustness of the reported results. We accept this recommendation and
provide the following clarifications and updates.
a) Clarification and augmentation of replicates in biochemical and molecular assays
In the original manuscript, figure legends stated “at least two” replicates,
primarily because a small subset of Western blot (WB) experiments had n = 2. In fact,
the vast majority of our WB, biochemical and molecular assays—such as SA-β-Gal
and EdU staining, flow cytometry, CCK-8 assays, quantitative PCR, cell migration,
and Transwell assays—were conducted with n = 3, and yielded statistically significant
results.
To further enhance statistical rigor in the revised manuscript, we have standardized
WB experiments to n = 3, increased other biochemical and molecular assays to n = 4,
and expanded the corresponding statistical analyses throughout the manuscript (e.g. Fig.
1a-b, d-e; Extended Data Fig. 1b, d-g, i; Extended Data Fig. 2a, b, d; Fig 6g-h; Extended
Data Fig. 19; Extended Data Fig. 20c-d;Fig. 7a-c, f-g; Fig 8h). The results demonstrate
that increasing biological replicates did not alter the conclusions; the findings remain
consistent with those in the original submission. We have also revised the figure legends
to explicitly report the exact number of biological replicates for each experiment.
b) Replicates and statistical justification in omics experiments
For proteomics: the OCPs quantitative proteomics in Fig. 2 includes n = 9
biological replicates, and the site-specific profiling of O-GlcNAc modifications on
OCPs in Fig. 5 includes n = 3, meeting accepted statistical standards for proteomic
analyses.
For next-generation sequencing: COGC-seq, RNA-seq, and DNA methylation
sequencing were performed with n = 2 biological replicates. We note that ENCODE
standards for ChIP-seq explicitly establish at least two independent biological replicates;
similarly, the ENCODE Whole-Genome Bisulfite Sequencing (WGBS) standards
specify at least two biological replicates per condition. Methodological studies further
indicate that, given appropriate sequencing depth and data quality, two biological
replicates generally provide robust performance for ChIP-seq peak identification and
reliable power for conventional RNA-seq differential expression analyses, while
acknowledging that additional replicates can improve sensitivity for small effects
(Nucleic Acids Research, 39(1), 190–201; Bioinformatics, 30(3), 301–304; Nature Cell
Biology, 22(7), 842–855, 2020). In our study, each assay included two independent
biological replicates and met commonly recommended depths: RNA-seq ≥ 20 million
mapped reads per sample, ChIP-seq ≥ 30 million uniquely mapped reads per sample,
and WGBS ≥ 200 million mapped reads per sample. All datasets passed standard quality
metrics (e.g., alignment rate, library complexity, duplication) with cross-replicate
consistency assessments. Analyses employed appropriate frameworks for high-
dimensional count data, using negative binomial–based models within standard
pipelines. Hence, our experimental design, sequencing depth, and statistical procedures
meet established standards and requirements.
c) Replicates in Molecular Dynamics Simulations
In the revised manuscript, we increased the number of independent molecular
dynamics (MD) simulation replicates by extending the trajectories to n = 3. The results
demonstrate good reproducibility across replicates, indicating that the MD findings are
robust.
d) Replicates in animal studies
In the original study, animal experiments were conducted with n = 6 biological
replicates. In the revised manuscript, we increased the number of biological replicates
for IHC staining to n = 6 and performed statistical analyses accordingly (Fig. 8f).
In summary, with the additional experiments and expanded reporting, the number
of biological replicates across our study now adheres to statistical requirements. The
results are statistically significant and consistently support our conclusions.
3. Quantification of differences in key experiments is missing – but it is required,
especially since the differences are not always clearly visible. For example, in Fig 1d-
e the panels are difficult to evaluate without proper quantification. In Fig 5i,
quantification of the IF stainings over multiple experiments is required, especially for
the GATAD2A part where DAPI staining does not appear to be of the same intensity,
as it should, between WT and S128A conditions. The same applies for Fig 7d-e where
a quantification and statistics are necessary for the interpretation of the shown results.
Reply：
We appreciate the reviewer’s observation that key experiments lacked quantitative
readouts. We accept this recommendation. Building on the increased number of
biological replicates, we have now provided quantitative analyses and statistical testing
for all relevant assays, including: SA-β-Gal staining (Fig. 1a, Fig. 1d, Extended Data
Fig. 1f, Fig. 7a); Flow cytometric analysis (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Fig. 1f, Extended
Data Fig. 2a, Fig. 7b); EdU staining (Fig. 1e, Extended Data Fig. 1d, Extended Data
Fig. 1i, Fig. 2b, Extended Data Fig. 20d); transwell co-culture assays (Fig. 7f); co-
culture wound-healing/scratch assays (Fig. 7g); IHC assays (Fig. 8h). The quantitative
results are consistent with, and further substantiate, the conclusions of this study.
Regarding the IF stainings in Fig. 5i, we agree with the reviewer’s concern.
Because the DAPI staining did not appear to have uniform intensity, we repeated the
experiment in the revised manuscript with n = 4. The new data show that DAPI intensity
is consistent across samples. Additionally, we quantified the colocalization in the IF
images using Pearson’s correlation coefficient. The quantitative analysis confirms that
O-GlcNAcylation modulates nuclear colocalization between JUN and SNF5, as well as
between GATAD2A and MBD2.
4. In lines 241-243 the authors mention that the chromatin states occupied by O-
GlcNAc increased in OIS by 20%, but this is not clear in any of the figure panels.
Please explain.
Reply：
We appreciate the reviewer’s attention to the statement in Fig. 3a regarding a “20%
increase” in chromatin states occupied by O-GlcNAc during OIS. In the revised
manuscript, we have clarified this description and annotated the figure to facilitate
interpretation.
Specifically, this result derives from an integrative analysis combining multiple
chromatin epigenetic marks with COGC-seq data to assess the genome-wide co-
occurrence of O-GlcNAc with or without distinct chromatin-state markers, using
ChromHMM. In Fig. 3a, the left panel summarizes changes in the genomic occupancy
of different chromatin states. The right panel provides a quantitative analysis, showing
that the summed fraction of O-GlcNAc-related chromatin states—defined as O-
GlcNAc promoter, O-GlcNAc enhancer, O-GlcNAc-repressed, and O-GlcNAc-
unmarked—increases as OIS progresses. Concretely, this aggregate fraction rose from
approximately 64.1% at D2 (O-GlcNAc promoter, 2.35%; O-GlcNAc enhancer, 0%;
O-GlcNAc-repressed, 0.51%; O-GlcNAc-unmarked, 61.25%) to approximately 83.5%
at D10 (O-GlcNAc promoter, 3.71%; O-GlcNAc enhancer, 0%; O-GlcNAc-repressed,
16.01%; O-GlcNAc-unmarked, 63.79%).
Accordingly, we have revised the text in the manuscript to read: “The fraction of
O-GlcNAc-related chromatin states can be categorized into four functional classes: O-
GlcNAc promoter, O-GlcNAc enhancer, O-GlcNAc occupied transcription-repressed
chromatin (O-GlcNAc-repressed), and those lacking any of the profiled histone
modifications (O-GlcNAc-unmarked). Consistent with the genome-wide elevation of
OCP binding, the cumulative fraction of chromatin states occupied by O-GlcNAc (i.e.,
the sum of O-GlcNAc promoter, O-GlcNAc-repressed, and O-GlcNAc-unmarked)
increased in OIS cells, from a minimum of 64.1% at D2 to a maximum of 83.5% at D10
of the genome”.
5. In lines 416-418 it is mentioned that the glycosylation restraint of JUN and
GATAD2A extinguished the chromatin accumulation of SNF5 and MBD2 at D10 when
OIS was fully established, but that is not accurate. A reduction of SNF5 and MBD2
levels (also requiring quantification) was observed both on D0 and D10.
Reply：
We appreciate the reviewer’s comment and agree that our original description of
how the chromatin binding of SNF5 and MBD2 is influenced by the glycosylation of
JUN and GATAD2A was not sufficiently precise. As shown in Fig. 6a, at both D0 and
D10, restraining the glycosylation of JUN and GATAD2A reduces their own chromatin
occupancy and concomitantly diminishes the chromatin association of their respective
interacting partners, SNF5 and MBD2. This observation directly supports the
conclusion that O-GlcNAcylation modulates the interactions between JUN–SNF5 and
GATAD2A–MBD2, which in turn accounts for the chromatin engagement of SNF5 and
MBD2. Given that our study focuses on the role of JUN and GATAD2A O-
GlcNAcylation during OIS progression, the ChIP-seq data at the D10 time point for
MBD2 and SNF5 in LU-RAS/KD-WT and LU-RAS/KD-AA cells (Fig. 6d) further
corroborate this mechanism.
In the revised manuscript, we have refined the sentence as follows: “Moreover,
restraining the glycosylation of JUN and GATAD2A diminishes the chromatin
accumulation of SNF5 and MBD2 at both D0 and D10, indicating a role for O-
GlcNAcylation in mediating the interactions and colocalization among these factors”.
6. In lines 442-444 the authors mention that compared to a “deficiency of O-GlcNAc”,
cells in D10 with JUNwt and GATAD2Awt overexpression showed a significant
decrease in cell cycle-related gene expression, however this is not clear. Is JUNwt and
GATAD2Awt overexpression sufficient to decrease the expression of cell cycle genes
regardless of O-GlcNAc levels? The authors need to address that.
Reply：
We thank the reviewer for raising the question of whether overexpression of
JUNWT and GATAD2AWT is sufficient to drive changes in cell-cycle and SASP-related
gene expression. In Fig. 6f, our RNA-seq analysis in LU-RAS/KD cells at the D10 time
point—where JUNWT and GATAD2AWT exhibit expression levels comparable to their
glycosylation-deficient mutants (Fig. 5d, f, h; Extended Data Fig. 14i)—shows that
differing glycosylation states of JUN and GATAD2A induce differential expression
across multiple cell‑cycle and SASP-associated genes. These findings indicate that O-
GlcNAcylation plays an important role in how JUN and GATAD2A regulate these
transcriptional programs.
To further distinguish the effects of O-GlcNAcylated JUN and GATAD2A from
those of the proteins per se, we extended the analyses in Fig. 6g by: (i) adding D10 LU-
RAS control groups to benchmark the impact of JUN and GATAD2A expression on
downstream target genes; and (ii) pharmacologically reducing O-GlcNAcylation with
OSMI-4 to assess the glycosylation dependence of the observed transcriptional effects.
At D10, relative to LU-RAS controls, knockdown of JUN and GATAD2A increased the
expression of cell-cycle genes (CCND1, STAG2, CDK6, E2F5) and decreased the
expression of SASP genes (IL6, IGFBP2, MIF, CXCL1). This finding is consistent with
prior reports that JUN and other AP-1 family transcription factors regulate SASP gene
expression and the progression of cellular senescence (Nature cell biology, 2020, 22(7):
842-855). Notably, OSMI-4–mediated reduction of O-GlcNAcylation significantly
increased the transcript levels of these cell-cycle genes while concomitantly decreasing
the mRNA levels of SASP genes (Fig. 6h and Extended Data Fig. 19b), closely
mirroring the effects observed upon JUN and GATAD2A knockdown in LU-RAS cells.
Collectively, these results support the conclusion that the O-GlcNAcylated forms of
JUN and GATAD2A—rather than the unglycosylated proteins alone—govern the
transcriptional regulation of cell-cycle and SASP gene expression. We have made
corresponding revisions at the relevant locations in the manuscript as well.
7. In lines 463-464 it is mentioned that SASP was restricted after reduction of O-
GlcNAc on JUN and GATAD2A, but this is unfortunately not experimentally tested.
No SASP marker alterations are shown via an appropriate assay. Some SASP factors
are examined in Fig. 8e, but that is in a different setting.
Reply：
We appreciate the reviewer’s observation that, in Fig. 7a–b, we did not directly
assess reductions in SASP following the reduction of O-GlcNAc on JUN and
GATAD2A in the senescence phenotype assays. We acknowledge that, in these
functional experiments, we did not measure the impact of altered O-GlcNAcylation of
JUN and GATAD2A on secreted SASP factors. Our inference regarding SASP
modulation was originally based on transcriptomic evidence under the same
experimental conditions (Fig. 6g), where multiple SASP genes showed altered
expression.
To strengthen the evidentiary basis for this conclusion, in the revised manuscript
we have added ELISA assays to quantify secreted SASP factors in conditioned media
from LU-RAS, LU-RAS/KD-WT, and LU-RAS/KD-AA cells, specifically measuring
IL6, IL1B, IGFBP2, MIF, TNFA, CXCL1, CXCL10, and CCL5. As shown in Fig. 7c,
reduction of O-GlcNAc on JUN and GATAD2A resulted in a significant decrease in the
secretion of multiple SASP factors, thereby corroborating our original interpretation
and aligning with the overall conclusions of the study. We have made corresponding
revisions at the relevant locations in the manuscript as well.
8. In Extended Data Fig 2a, the presented data does not appear to be in line with Fig 1e
where TMG treatment decreased EdU+ cells. Please explain.
Reply：
We thank the reviewer for raising the point regarding the interpretation of our EdU
staining results. EdU (5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine) is a thymidine analog that is
incorporated into newly synthesized DNA. In this study, EdU was not present
continuously during senescence induction. Instead, for each assay we added EdU only
during a 2-hour pulse immediately prior to fixation at the indicated time points along
the senescence time course (D0–D10). Consequently, as senescence progresses and
proliferation diminishes, DNA replication is increasingly suppressed, leading to a lower
fraction of EdU-positive cells. In Extended Data Fig. 2a, TMG treatment induced
cell-cycle arrest, which is consistent with the reduced proportion of EdU-positive cells
observed in Fig. 1e.
To preclude misinterpretation, we have revised the Methods to more explicitly
describe the EdU staining protocol, as follows.
For EdU staining, representative samples from the senescence time series were
analyzed for EdU incorporation using the Click-iT EdU Alexa Fluor Imaging Kit
(Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Cells were
seeded in 6-well plates and cultured under senescence-inducing conditions to the
indicated time points (D0, D2, D4, D10). Immediately prior to fixation, cells were
pulsed with EdU for 2 h. After incubation, the medium was aspirated, and cells were
washed twice with PBS and fixed with paraformaldehyde. Cells were then washed three
times with washing buffer (PBS containing 3% BSA) and permeabilized with 0.3%
Triton X-100 for 15 min. Following three additional washes with washing buffer, cells
were incubated with the Click Reaction Mixture. For nuclear counterstaining, Hoechst
dye was added at a final concentration of 1 μg/mL and incubated for 10 min at 25 °C in
the dark. Excess dye was removed by washing with PBS prior to imaging. Cells
exhibiting both green (EdU) and blue (Hoechst) signals were scored as EdU-positive.
9. Regarding the pull-down assays in Fig 4d and Extended Data Fig 11, proper IgG
controls should be included there. Also, the rationale behind using sWGA for the pull-
down assay should be presented in the main text.
Reply：
We appreciate the reviewer’s comment regarding the absence of appropriate
controls in our immunoprecipitation (IP) and pull-down experiments. We have
incorporated the suggested controls in the revised manuscript. Specifically, we added
IgG controls or IgG-conjugated magnetic bead controls to the IP assays presented in
Fig. 4d, 4e, 5d, 5e, 5f, 5h, and 5j. In addition, we introduced a negative control in
Extended Data Fig. 11a by using agarose beads lacking succinylated wheat germ
agglutinin (sWGA) lectin to rule out nonspecific binding to the matrix.
Our study employs complementary orthogonal approaches to demonstrate
O-GlcNAc modification across multiple members of the NuRD and SWI/SNF
complexes: i) Metabolically labeled proteomics to detect O-GlcNAc at the proteome
level. ii) Classical biochemical IP using O-GlcNAc–specific antibodies. iii)
Lectin-based pull-down employing sWGA, which binds O-GlcNAc and has been
reported to offer improved specificity for O-GlcNAc–modified proteins relative to
WGA (RSC advances, 2023, 13(1): 264-280; Clinical proteomics, 2014, 11(1): 8). The
convergence of these methods provides robust, cross-validated evidence that several
subunits of the NuRD and SWI/SNF complexes are O-GlcNAcylated.
To further strengthen the evidentiary basis for the sWGA pull-down results, we
optimized the workflow in the revised manuscript by adapting procedures described in
the literature (Nature Communications, 2025, 16(1): 5959). In brief, we first performed
IP of GATAD2A and JUN in OIS LU-RAS cells, eluted the bound proteins, and then
subjected the eluates to sWGA-agarose pull-down. The pull-down products were

In the revised manuscript, we have expanded the Methods to delineate each critical
step. Briefly, cells were crosslinked with formaldehyde to stabilize proteins interacting
with chromatin in preparation for proteomic and DNA cis‑element analyses. We then
performed cytoplasm–nucleus fractionation using a hypotonic buffer in which the
principal lytic component was an optimized 0.4% Igepal CA‑630 (v/v). Nuclear pellets

NaCl; 1.5 mM MgCl ; 0.2 mM EDTA; 10% glycerol; 0.4% Igepal CA‑630 (v/v);
2

2
(v/v); 0.1% SDS (w/v)). Chromatin was fragmented by sonication and centrifuged at

In the original manuscript, several figure legends stated “at least two” replicates,

appropriate frameworks for high-dimensional count data, using negative binomial–

Reply：
We appreciate the reviewer’s observation that different cell types in our study
exhibit distinct cell-cycle arrest states after OIS. While senescence-associated arrest
typically occurs in G1 or G2/M, prior studies have also reported S-phase arrest,
likely reflecting cell-type specificity and the particular modality by which senescence is
induced. For example, in MCF10A breast epithelial cells—the same line used in our
study—aphidicolin-induced senescence has been reported to associate with S-phase
arrest, accompanied by canonical senescence markers such as elevated SA-β-gal
activity, nuclear enlargement, and increased p21 (Cell death & disease, 2014, 5(7):
e1351-e1351). In the revised manuscript, we clarify these context-specific differences
and provide appropriate citations. “LU-RAS and SK-RAS fibroblasts undergoing OIS
exhibit G2/M arrest, consistent with many established features of cellular senescence.
By contrast, MCF-RAS epithelial cells arrest in S phase, in agreement with prior reports
(Cell death & disease, 2014, 5(7): e1351-e1351), and HaC-RAS epithelial cells show
a similar S-phase arrest. These differences may reflect cell-type–specific programs and
the distinct modalities by which senescence is induced.”
We also appreciate the reviewer’s comment regarding the lack of correlation
between EdU labeling and FACS analysis for MCF-RAS and HaC-RAS cells. EdU
(5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine) is a thymidine analog incorporated into newly synthesized
DNA and thus reports active DNA replication during the labeling interval. In our study,
EdU was not present continuously throughout senescence induction. Instead, for each
assay we administered a 2-hour EdU pulse immediately prior to fixation at the indicated
time points along the senescence time course (D0-D10). As senescence advances and
proliferative capacity declines, DNA replication becomes increasingly suppressed,
yielding a reduced fraction of EdU-positive cells during the short pulse window. In
Extended Data Fig. 1i, both MCF-RAS and HaC-RAS epithelial cells are arrested in S
phase at D10. At this stage, despite S-phase DNA content detected by FACS, ongoing
DNA synthesis during the brief EdU pulse is minimal, resulting in few EdU-positive
cells. This mechanistic distinction—DNA content versus active DNA synthesis—
accounts for the observed discrepancy between FACS profiles and EdU incorporation
at late senescence time points.
To preclude misinterpretation, we have revised the Methods to more explicitly
describe the EdU staining protocol, as follows:
For EdU staining, representative samples from the senescence time series were
analyzed for EdU incorporation using the Click-iT EdU Alexa Fluor Imaging Kit
(Thermo Fisher Scientific) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Cells were
seeded in 6-well plates and cultured under senescence-inducing conditions to the
indicated time points (D0, D2, D4, D10). Immediately prior to fixation, cells were
pulsed with EdU for 2 h. After incubation, the medium was aspirated, and cells were
washed twice with PBS and fixed with paraformaldehyde. Cells were then washed three
times with washing buffer (PBS containing 3% BSA) and permeabilized with 0.3%
Triton X-100 for 15 min. Following three additional washes with washing buffer, cells
were incubated with the Click Reaction Mixture. For nuclear counterstaining, Hoechst
dye was added at a final concentration of 1 μg/mL and incubated for 10 min at 25 °C in
the dark. Excess dye was removed by washing with PBS prior to imaging. Cells
exhibiting both green (EdU) and blue (Hoechst) signals were scored as EdU-positive.

gene is downregulated at the transcriptomic level during OIS progression
(approximately two-fold), while OGT protein levels appear elevated on Western blot
(Fig. 1c), suggesting a possible post-transcriptional regulation. The current statement
in the discussion (lines 538–539) remains vague and insufficiently refered to the data
presented. Moreover, it is striking that no decrease in OGT protein levels is observed
upon treatment with 50 µM Thiamet-G (which is a very high concentration compared
to what is generally used in other cell lines), and conversely, no increase in OGT is seen
with OSMI-4 treatment (Fig. 1f), despite the literature describing compensatory

Reply：
We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the discrepancy
between OGT transcript and protein levels during OIS. In LU-RAS cells, we observed
an approximately twofold reduction in OGT mRNA across the OIS time course,
whereas OGT protein levels were increased by Western blot (Fig. 1c). As the reviewer
suggested, this divergence likely reflects post-transcriptional regulation, including
altered protein stability.
To directly address this, we have added new experiments in the revised manuscript
(Extended Data Fig. 4c) assessing OGT protein half-life during OIS. Using
cycloheximide chase, we compared OGT half-life at D0 versus D10 and further
evaluated the role of proteolytic degradation with MG132. We found that OGT half-life
is prolonged during OIS, and MG132 treatment led to a further increase in OGT protein
abundance. These results support a model in which enhanced OGT stability contributes
to the observed increase in OGT protein despite reduced transcript levels. In parallel,
our data in Fig. 1c and Fig. 1d show that pharmacological modulation of global
O-GlcNAcylation does not appreciably alter OGT protein abundance. Although OGT
itself has been reported to be O-GlcNAc-modified (Journal of Biological Chemistry,
2000, 275(15): 10983-10988; Biochemical and biophysical research communications,
2018, 499(2): 354-360), our findings indicate that the OIS-associated changes in OGT
stability are largely independent of O-GlcNAc levels. We have incorporated this
interpretation and the new stability data into the revised Discussion.
We appreciate the reviewer’s comment regarding the apparent insensitivity of OGT
protein abundance to pharmacological modulation with Thiamet-G and OSMI-4. While
prior studies have reported that changing homeostatic O-GlcNAc levels can influence
OGT protein levels (Annual review of biochemistry, 2011, 80(1): 825-858), in our
system we did not observe compensatory changes in OGT protein following treatment
with either compound. We propose that, although the relatively high concentrations of
Thiamet-G and OSMI-4 used here effectively modulate OGA and OGT activity,
compensatory regulation is highly dependent on cell type and stress context and may
manifest at the level of UDP-GlcNAc substrate flux rather than as changes in OGT
abundance. For example, in our previous work, chemotherapeutic stimulation of MCF-7
breast cancer cells markedly increased flux through the hexosamine biosynthetic
pathway (HBP, Cell death & disease, 2018, 9(5): 485), elevating the glycosyl donor
UDP-GlcNAc and thereby enhancing global protein O-GlcNAcylation, despite no
detectable changes in OGT or OGA protein expression. Although OGT itself can be
O-GlcNAc–modified, in the present study Thiamet-G and OSMI-4 robustly altered
cellular O-GlcNAcylation without measurably changing OGT protein abundance. These
findings suggest that the OIS-associated changes in OGT protein abundance are largely
independent of O-GlcNAc levels. We have expanded the Discussion in the revised
manuscript to address potential compensatory mechanisms underlying this issue.
We appreciate the reviewer’s comment regarding Fig. 4d. In the revised
manuscript, we have added pan-O-GlcNAc Western blots for all experiments involving
OGT inhibitors, including Fig. 4d and Extended Data Fig. 11a. The pan-O-GlcNAc
Western blots for Fig. 4e have been provided in the revised Fig. 4d.

Response to Reviewers
Reviewer 1#
1. In Fig 5i, the IF panels showing only one cell at a time are still not convincing, as it
is impossible to observe actual differences across the conditions. It is surprising that
Pearson’s coefficient and the corresponding plots so strongly indicate the opposite to
what the images display.
Reply：
We thank the reviewer for this comment. We would like to clarify the rationale and
robustness of the colocalization analysis presented in Fig. 5i:
(1) In the previously revised manuscript, we presented immunofluorescence images of
individual cells captured using high magnification confocal microscopy. This
approach ensures high-resolution visualization of colocalization between O-
GlcNAc modified proteins in the nucleus. For quantitative analysis, we followed
established methods using Scatter J plugin in Image J software. The reference for
developing this plugin is Journal of Open Research Software, 2016, 4(1): e5-e5.
The software defines that a set of datapoints is formed out of the grey values of
pixels at the same position in the different input images. Therefore, a datapoint
contains the results of all measurements taken at the corresponding position. Each
datapoint corresponds to a pixel position in the spatial domain. Specifically, the
green signal intensity of MBD2 or SNF5 was plotted on the Y-axis, and the red
signal intensity of Flag-GATAD2A or HA-JUN on the X-axis. Despite showing
only a single cell, each nucleus contains numerous spots, providing statistically
meaningful data. Notably, this single-cell, spot-based colocalization analysis is
widely applied in the literature and has been shown to be statistically robust
(Autophagy. 2022;18(5):990-1004; Cancer research. 2025;85(17):3313-3334). We
have updated the Fig. 5i legend to clarify the meaning of the quantitative analysis.
(2) In our previous study, we also conducted experiments using lower-magnification
confocal microscopy to capture multiple cells within the same field of view, and
this result has been presented in the response letter below. These images confirmed
that O-GlcNAc modification significantly affects colocalization of Flag-
GATAD2A with MBD2, and HA-JUN with SNF5. However, due to limited
resolution, it was difficult to accurately distinguish the fine nuclear colocalization
regions necessary for precise quantitative analysis. By contrast, the high-
magnification single-cell images in the previously revised figure provide more
detailed and reliable visualization of nuclear protein complex localization, suitable
for quantitative statistics.
(3) In addition to the immunofluorescence data in Fig. 5i, other experiments, including
co-IP and pulldown assays (Fig. 4e, Fig. 5f–h) and ChIP-seq analyses (Fig. 6b–d),
consistently demonstrate interactions between GATAD2A and MBD2, and
between JUN and SNF5. Together, these independent lines of evidence support the
reliability of the colocalization results presented in Fig. 5i.
(4) The reviewer pointed out that “the Pearson’s coefficient and the corresponding
plots strongly indicate the opposite of what the images display.” In response, we
suggest that the reviewer refer to the high-resolution colocalization images we have
provided for further evaluation. After mutation of the O-GlcNAc sites, the
interactions between GATAD2A and MBD2, as well as between JUN and SNF5,
were markedly reduced; however, these proteins remained localized within the
nucleus. Colocalization is indicated when green and red fluorescence signals (spots)
overlap at the same position within a given region, whereas a lack of complete
overlap between the two signals at the same pixel suggests the absence of
colocalization. By analyzing the overlap of all nuclear pixels, the Pearson’s
correlation coefficient was calculated, where an R value of 1 represents perfect
colocalization and an R value of 0 indicates no colocalization. Our results show
that O-GlcNAc modified GATAD2A and JUN exhibit a high degree of
colocalization with their respective complex partners, MBD2 and SNF5. In
contrast, mutation of the O-GlcNAc glycosylation sites in GATAD2A and JUN
significantly diminished their colocalization with these interacting partners,
suggesting that O-GlcNAc modification plays an essential regulatory role in
maintaining these protein protein interactions.
2. The blots in Fig 5 unfortunately remain problematic. Although the authors in their
responses mention the incorporation of IgG controls (they actually show them in the
IPs of Fig 4), these controls are still missing from Fig 5 and Extended Data Figs.
Reply：
We would like to thank the reviewer for raising the question regarding the IgG
control in Fig. 5 and the corresponding extended figures. During the revision of our
previous manuscript, we had already considered this issue raised by the reviewer and
included additional experiments in the revised version to provide the necessary IgG
control groups. We offer the following explanations for the IgG control in Fig. 5 and
the corresponding extended figures.
(1) In the co-IP experiments in Fig. 5 d–f, h, j and Extended Data Fig. 14 b–c, where
we expressed Flag-tagged GATAD2A or HA-tagged JUN, we used commercially
available Flag or HA tag antibody-conjugated magnetic beads. These beads were
coupled with high-quality mouse monoclonal IgG antibodies via covalent bonding.
Due to the covalent fixation of the antibodies to the bead surface, they cannot be
easily eluted, which means that almost no IgG will detach from the beads during
the experiment. As a result, IgG heavy or light chains are not detected in
subsequent immunoblotting experiments. This characteristic has been supported
by several published studies, including our previous work (Nature communications,
2020, 11, 5898，Nature Communications, 2025, 16, 4792; Nature Communications,
2025, 16, 5959).
(2) Additionally, even if a small amount of coupled IgG is eluted from the beads, to
avoid interference from IgG, we used antibodies from different species in the
subsequent immunoblotting detection following the co-IP experiments in Fig. 5 d–
f, h, j and Extended Data Fig. 14 b–c. These antibodies included anti-Flag, anti-
HA, anti-SNF5, anti-MBD2, anti-MTA1, anti-CHD4, and anti-SMRC1, all of
which are rabbit-derived antibodies. This has been noted in the figure legend of the
current revision. Previous studies have shown that using antibodies from different
species can effectively prevent IgG interference (Nature Communications, 2025,
16, 227; Nature Communications, 2024, 15, 7398, Oncogene. 2023;42(30):2329-
2346). To meet the requirements for control groups, we included empty vector
groups (vehicle) as negative controls in all IP-Flag and IP-HA experiments. No
corresponding bands were detected in the vehicle group using immunomagnetic
beads, confirming the reliability of the positive bands obtained in the experiment.
Although no IgG control was included in these experiments, the same amount of
immunomagnetic beads (60 μL) was used consistently across all experimental
groups to ensure consistency in experimental conditions and the reliability of
results. This description has been added to the corresponding figure legends and
"Methods" section of the revised manuscript.
(3) For the immunoblotting results using Flag or HA tag antibody conjugated magnetic
beads, we have included the raw data (full membrane with an adequate molecular
weight range at both the upper and lower ends) in the source data. Below, we
present some of the results, showing that using immunomagnetic beads and
subsequent immunoblotting with antibodies from different species indeed does not
detect IgG heavy or light chains.
In summary, based on the results and evidence provided, we believe that the co-IP
experimental results in Fig. 5 and the corresponding extended figures are reliable.
3. I still disagree with the authors that the data presented in Fig 1e and Ext Data Fig 2a
are in accordance with one another. In Fig 1e, EU staining labels proliferating cells (in
S phase). That proportion of cells evidently decreases upon TMG treatment. On the
contrary, Ext Data Fig 2a shows an elevated S phase in MCF-RAS cells. The authors
should provide a reasonable explanation. Most of the experiments were performed in
LU-RAS cells, and differences such as this one may raise concerns regarding cell line
bias and data reproducibility.
Reply：
The reviewer has raised concerns regarding the EdU staining and cell cycle
experimental results in OIS cells, as well as the regulation mechanisms of different
types of cells undergoing distinct cell cycle arrest. We offer the following further
explanations:
(1) As the reviewer correctly pointed out, EdU staining is a classic method used to
label cells in the DNA synthesis phase (S phase), and it is often employed to reflect
cellular proliferative activity. In this study, the EdU staining protocol followed a
standard procedure. The reference for developing this method is Cytometry Part A,
2009, 75(6): 535–546. Following this method, we add EdU to the cell culture dish
2 hours before detection. This method is based on established protocols (Cell, 2016,
173(6): 1370–1384.e16; Cell, 2016, 167(5): 1264–1280.e18) and has been
previously described in our earlier manuscript.
(2) In this study, all EdU staining experiments were conducted on cells that had already
undergone senescence induction. These OIS cells exhibited senescence phenotypes
and had mostly undergone cell cycle arrest, halting proliferation before EdU was
added. We acknowledge that different types of senescence may involve arrest at
distinct phases of the cell cycle, as confirmed by the flow cytometry results in this
study. However, it is important to note that these senescent cells had lost their DNA
replication capability prior to the EdU staining, and thus no DNA synthesis occurs
in the S phase. As a result, they were unable to incorporate EdU and exhibited EdU
negative staining. Therefore, the EdU staining experiment in this study cannot be
directly correlated with the flow cytometry cell cycle arrest results but serves to
confirm whether the cells have ceased proliferating, acting as one of the markers
of cellular senescence.
(3) In Fig. 1b, e, and Extended Data Fig. 2a, we observed that LU-RAS cells primarily
arrest in the G2 phase following senescence, while MCF-RAS cells arrest in the S
phase. TMG treatment increased cell cycle arrest in both LU-RAS and MCF-RAS
cells at the D4 time point, indicating that O-GlcNAc modification plays a
regulatory role in the senescence phenotype. It is essential to clarify that before
performing the EdU staining, these cells had already entered a state of cell cycle
arrest. Regardless of whether the cells arrested in the S phase or G2 phase, the
arrested cells (which represent different proportions in the experimental groups)
lost their proliferative capacity and were unable to incorporate EdU, resulting in
EdU negative staining. These results reflect that the EdU negative status
corresponds to the loss of proliferative activity, rather than reflecting differences
in specific cell cycle arrest phases.
(4) Moreover, although we observed that different cell types undergo different cell
cycle arrest states following OIS induction, the primary focus of this study is not
to investigate the differences in cell cycle arrest at different phases, but to explore
the overall regulatory function and mechanisms of O-GlcNAc modification in
cellular senescence. Most of the mechanistic studies were conducted using LU-
RAS cells. Overall, our multi-omics analysis results consistently suggest that O-
GlcNAc modification promotes cell cycle arrest and senescence by suppressing the
transcription of several cell cycle related genes, such as CCND1, STAG2, E2F5,
and CDK6. While the O-GlcNAc regulated cell cycle-related genes in LU-RAS
cells may differ from those in MCF-RAS cells, which could explain why different
cell types arrest in distinct cell cycle phases, the core molecular mechanism by
which O-GlcNAc modification regulates cell cycle factor transcription to alter the
senescence phenotype remains consistent. Thus, even though different cell types
may exhibit distinct phases of cycle arrest during senescence, the underlying
mechanism is attributed to the transcriptional repression of cell cycle factors
mediated by O-GlcNAc modification. Therefore, we are confident that despite
differences in cell cycle arrest mechanisms across cell lines, the regulatory role of
O-GlcNAc modification on cell cycle factors during senescence is consistent. This
discussion has been further elaborated upon in the revised manuscript.
